paragraphs: Nikanor, in the Second Temple period, is mentioned in Mishnah as pious. Middot 1 and 2: a gateway in the courtyard is Nikanor's Gate, with two small wickets, right and left; likewise Shekalim 6. It faces the Holy of Holies; hence Berakhot forbids levity facing it. Sotah 1: there they administer the suspected adulteresses' water and purify women after childbirth and lepers. Keitzad Tzolin: the gateways were not sanctified, so lepers can stand there and reach their hands inside for the rite performed on their thumbs. Yoma 3 and Tosefta 2: miracles happened to his doors, and he is praised. He went to Alexandria in Egypt and made two bronze doors. At sea a storm struck the sailors; they threw one overboard to lighten the ship and wished to throw the second. He tied himself to it, saying they must throw him with it. The sea calmed. He grieved for the lost door, but the sea cast it where the pious man landed. Some say a great fish swallowed and disgorged it. Middot 2: all the gates were changed to gold except Nikanor's, because of their miracles; some say because they gleamed like gold. Yosippon ben Guryon says it was named because they killed Nikanor the Greek commander there and hung him on the gate in Hasmonean days; end of Ta'anit 2 likewise suggests this.
